name: Ferrocerium rod
summary: Scraped metal sparks at around 3,000 C — the ignition source that works wet, cold, at altitude, and thousands of times.

steps.text: Prepare the tinder bundle first and put it where the sparks will fall. Never strike before the tinder is ready.
Scrape the rod hard with a 90-degree edge — the spine of a knife, not the blade.
steps.why: A sharp edge slices the rod instead of shaving off the burning swarf, and dulls your blade for nothing.

steps.text: Hold the rod tip almost touching the tinder and pull the ROD back under a stationary striker, rather than pushing the striker at the tinder.
steps.why: Pushing the striker scatters the sparks and knocks the nest apart with the follow-through.

steps.text: Once it catches, close the bundle loosely and blow it to flame.

verify: Fat orange sparks that stay burning after they land mean you are scraping hard enough. Thin white flashes mean too light a touch.
A rod that will not spark usually has its factory lacquer still on — scrape that off first.
limits: A ferro rod throws sparks, not flame. It cannot light wood, paper towel, or anything coarser than fine fibre.
It is a manufactured item. When it is gone, `fire-bow-drill` is the fallback, which is why the fallback is worth practising while you still have the rod.
cautions: The swarf burns hot enough to melt synthetic clothing. Do not strike over a jacket you are wearing.
